title: The Bible: Inspiration and Authority
summary: Why Christians believe the Bible is God's Word, and what that means for how we trust and obey it.
description: This course studies the doctrine of Scripture. It explains what the Bible claims about itself, what inspiration means, why the Bible can be trusted, and why it is the final authority for faith and life. Each truth is drawn from the Bible's own words and applied to the life of an ordinary believer.
objectives: Show what the Bible teaches about its own inspiration
Explain why Scripture is true and trustworthy in all it affirms
Establish the authority and sufficiency of Scripture over every other source
Encourage daily, obedient use of the Bible
outcomes: Explain inspiration using 2 Timothy 3:16 and 2 Peter 1:21
Define infallibility and inerrancy in simple words
Show why Scripture judges tradition, experience and prophecy
Explain the sufficiency and clarity of Scripture
Build a habit of reading, believing and obeying the Bible

modules.title: God-Breathed: Inspiration
modules.intro: What does it mean that the Bible is inspired? This week we look at the Bible's own claims.

lessons.title: All Scripture is given by inspiration
lessons.body:
Paul writes, "All scripture is given by inspiration of God" (2 Timothy 3:16). The Greek word means "God-breathed". Scripture is not merely inspiring, like a good poem. It is breathed out by God, as truly as His own spoken word.

This covers *all* Scripture, not only the parts that seem important to us. Jesus said, "the scripture cannot be broken" (John 10:35), and that not one jot or tittle would pass from the law (Matthew 5:18).

Because the Bible comes from God, it carries His authority and His truthfulness.

lessons.title: Holy men moved by the Holy Ghost
lessons.body:
How did God give His Word through human writers? Peter answers: "holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost" (2 Peter 1:21). The word *moved* pictures a ship carried along by the wind.

God did not usually dictate like a typist. Moses, David, Luke and Paul wrote in their own styles and from their own experience (Luke 1:1-3). Yet the Spirit so guided them that what they wrote was exactly what God intended.

This is called *verbal, plenary* inspiration: the very words (verbal) of all Scripture (plenary) are from God.

lessons.title: What Jesus believed about Scripture
lessons.body:
The strongest reason to trust the Bible is Jesus' own view of it. He quoted the Old Testament as final: "It is written" (Matthew 4:4). He treated its history as real: Adam and Eve, Noah, Jonah (Matthew 19:4-5; 24:37; 12:40).

He also promised the apostles that the Spirit would bring His words to their remembrance and guide them into all truth (John 14:26; 16:13). This is the basis of the New Testament.

If we follow Christ as Lord, we must share His trust in Scripture.

The teaching that the very words of Scripture, not only its ideas, are inspired.
The teaching that all of Scripture, every part, is inspired.
The mistaken idea that the writers were mere typists with no part of their own.
One sent personally by Christ with authority to teach His church.
The meaning of the Greek word translated 'given by inspiration' in 2 Timothy 3:16.

The writers spoke as they were carried along by the Holy Ghost.
Scripture cannot be broken.
Jesus lived by every word that proceeds from God's mouth.

modules.title: True and Trustworthy
modules.intro: If God breathed out Scripture, it shares His truthfulness. This week we study infallibility and inerrancy.

lessons.title: God cannot lie
lessons.body:
Scripture's truthfulness rests on God's character. God "cannot lie" (Titus 1:2), and "it was impossible for God to lie" (Hebrews 6:18). Jesus prayed, "thy word is truth" (John 17:17).

If the Bible is God's Word, then whatever it affirms is true. "Every word of God is pure" (Proverbs 30:5). The psalmist says God's words are "as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times" (Psalm 12:6).

So when Scripture speaks about God, salvation, history or human life, we may rely on it completely.

lessons.title: Infallible and inerrant
lessons.body:
Two words help us say this clearly. **Infallible** means Scripture cannot fail or mislead us in what it teaches. **Inerrant** means it contains no error in anything it affirms, as originally given.

Inerrancy does not mean the Bible uses modern scientific language. It speaks of the sun rising, as we still do. It uses round numbers, free quotations and ordinary descriptions. Truthfulness is judged by what the writer meant to say.

It applies to the original writings. Copies and translations are faithful to the degree that they match those originals, and God has preserved His Word remarkably well (1 Peter 1:25).

lessons.title: Handling hard passages
lessons.body:
Some passages seem difficult: numbers that differ between Kings and Chronicles, or Gospel accounts told from different angles. Faithful readers have found careful answers to most of these, often by reading the context, the purpose of each writer, or the way ancient writers summarised.

Where we do not yet know the answer, humility is wise. "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us" (Deuteronomy 29:29).

A difficulty is not the same as an error. Our understanding is limited; God's Word is not.

terms.def: Scripture cannot fail or lead astray in what it teaches.
Scripture, as originally given, is without error in all that it affirms.
The original writings of the biblical books, as first written.
God's perfect faithfulness to what is real; He cannot lie.
Describing things as they appear, such as the sun rising.
A passage we do not yet fully understand, which is not the same as an error.

texts.teaches: God cannot lie.
God's word is truth.

Inerrancy allows for ordinary language, round numbers and different viewpoints.
Difficulties call for humility and careful study, not doubt.

options: The character of God, who cannot lie

modules.title: The Final Authority
modules.intro: This week we see why Scripture stands above tradition, experience and every other voice.

lessons.title: To the law and to the testimony
lessons.body:
God's people are to test every message by His written Word. "To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them" (Isaiah 8:20).

Jesus rebuked religious leaders for "making the word of God of none effect through your tradition" (Mark 7:13). Tradition can be helpful, but it must bow to Scripture.

The same is true of experiences, dreams and prophecies today. Paul says, "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1 Thessalonians 5:21). The Bible is the measuring rod for everything else.

lessons.title: Sufficient for faith and life
lessons.body:
Scripture is **sufficient**: it contains all that God's people need to know for salvation and for living to please Him. It makes us "wise unto salvation" and "throughly furnished unto all good works" (2 Timothy 3:15-17). God's divine power "hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness" (2 Peter 1:3).

This does not mean the Bible tells us which job to take. It means it gives the principles for every decision, and we need no further revelation to know the way of salvation or the will of God for holy living.

So we must not add to it or take from it (Revelation 22:18-19).

lessons.title: Clear and necessary
lessons.body:
Scripture is **clear** in its main message. "The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple" (Psalm 119:130). Some parts are hard (2 Peter 3:16), but the way of salvation and the duties of life can be understood by ordinary believers who read with prayer.

Scripture is also **necessary**. Without it we could know that God exists, but not how to be saved. "Faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God" (Romans 10:17).

This is why the Bible should be translated into every language and taught in every home.

modules.title: Living by the Word
modules.intro: Believing in the Bible's authority must change how we read, hear and obey it. This week is practical.

lessons.title: Reading and meditating
lessons.body:
The blessed person delights in the law of the LORD and meditates on it "day and night" (Psalm 1:2). Joshua was told the book of the law should not depart out of his mouth (Joshua 1:8).

Meditation means slowly turning a passage over in the mind: reading it again, asking what it says about God, about us and about how to live, and praying it back to God.

A simple plan helps: a regular time, a set passage, a notebook, and one truth to carry into the day.

lessons.title: Hearing and obeying
lessons.body:
Jesus ended the Sermon on the Mount with two builders. The wise man "heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them" (Matthew 7:24). The storm showed the difference.

James warns against hearing without doing, like a man who looks in a mirror and forgets his face (James 1:22-25). Authority means the Bible is to be obeyed, not just admired.

Obedience is not a way to earn salvation, but the fruit of loving Christ: "If ye love me, keep my commandments" (John 14:15).

lessons.title: Hiding the Word in the heart
lessons.body:
"Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee" (Psalm 119:11). Memorising Scripture arms us against temptation, as Jesus answered Satan three times with "It is written" (Matthew 4:1-10).

The Word also comforts in trouble (Psalm 119:50), guides decisions (Psalm 119:105) and equips us to share the gospel.

Start small: one verse a week, written on a card, repeated morning and evening. Over a year, that is more than fifty verses stored for life.

terms.def: Thinking slowly and prayerfully over a passage so it shapes the heart.
Doing what God's Word commands, out of love for Christ.
Storing Scripture in the mind and heart by repetition.
Regular personal reading of the Bible for worship and growth.
Someone who listens to the Word but does not put it into practice.
A picture of God's Word giving guidance for each step of life.

texts.teaches: The blessed person delights in God's law and meditates on it day and night.
The wise builder hears Christ's words and does them.

short.q: Explain what 2 Timothy 3:16 teaches about Scripture.
short.model: All Scripture is breathed out by God, so every part carries His authority and is profitable for teaching and righteousness.

short.q: How did God use human writers without their words being merely human?
short.model: The Holy Ghost carried the writers along so that, while they used their own styles and experience, what they wrote was exactly God's word.
Inerrancy means Scripture, as originally given, is without error in everything it affirms.

short.q: What does the sufficiency of Scripture mean?
short.model: Scripture contains everything we need to know for salvation and for living a godly life, so nothing needs to be added to it.

short.q: Why must tradition and experience be tested by Scripture?
short.model: Because Scripture alone is God's word and final authority, while traditions and experiences are human and can mislead.

short.q: Why did Jesus' view of Scripture matter for Christians?
short.model: Jesus trusted and quoted Scripture as fully true ('It is written'; 'the scripture cannot be broken'), and His followers should share His view.
